articles.title: Tensions with teachers, pupils and Turkiye: Inside Azerbaijan’s hijab row
articles.summary: Teachers fear losing their livelihoods and students risk being excluded as Baku’s close ally appears critical.
articles.body:
For Gulshan Aliyeva, a teacher, the debate over the hijab in Azerbaijan’s public schools has become a personal struggle that threatens her career and her daughter’s education.

This week, the English teacher went to her school in Baku wearing her headscarf, but was denied entry. Her daughter was also prevented from entering, she told Al Jazeera.

“I want to fulfil my responsibilities, educate students and continue my career without my religious beliefs becoming an obstacle to my employment,” said Aliyeva, who has 23 years of experience.

She argued that Azerbaijan’s Labour Code, specifically Article 16, prohibits discrimination in employment in the country.

Last month, new rules stopped short of explicitly singling out the hijab but banned pupils from wearing clothes that violate the principle of secularism in education.

Protests have erupted over the issue in a country where more than 90 percent are Muslim.

Aliyeva is among several teachers and students who have been denied entry; the Ministry of Internal Affairs said on Monday that 37 people had been detained for disrupting public order while breaking the new rules.

“Our constitutional rights to work and receive an education without obstruction must be upheld,” said Aliyeva, who intends to continue reporting to work. She said she will take her case to the relevant authorities if necessary.

The Baku City Education Department has announced that schools will be monitored to assess compliance.

Sheikh-ul-Islam Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board (CMB), told local media on Tuesday that the hijab is “an important religious obligation”.

While people “cannot oppose the decisions of the state” they can express their “views as citizens”, he added, but criticised protesters for disturbing schools.

He also said the issue was being used for political purposes, while urging critics to address relevant ministers.

Not everyone believes the restrictions represent an infringement of individual rights.

Baku resident Timur Rzayev believes the controversy has been politicised. In his view, the government’s uniform policy should be adhered to “rather than debated”.

“There is a government decision on the implementation of uniform dress codes,” he said.

Rzayev opposes girls under the age of 18 wearing the hijab, saying such a decision often reflects parental preferences rather than the wishes of the children themselves.

His position reflects a wider concern among some Azerbaijanis that religious practices should not mix with public education.

“We are a secular state that respects the rights of religious people,” he said.

During the Soviet era, the state restricted religious practices and did not allow people to freely observe their religious traditions. After independence, these restrictions were eased, allowing people greater freedom to practise their faith.

Natiq Jafarli, head of the opposition REAL Party, said that the question of students wearing the hijab warrants further discussion.

“The issue concerning female students needs to be discussed. Public schools should establish certain compromise arrangements for primary school pupils,” he said.

“Teachers are adults, and imposing restrictions on how they dress is the wrong approach,” he added.

The controversy has also affected Azerbaijan’s closest relationship on the international stage.

Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said Azerbaijan’s move was “unacceptable”.

“Leaving a student who covers her head for reasons of faith at the school gate – how can this fit into any conscience, any sense of justice?” he posted on X.

The governing Yeni Azerbaijan Party (YAP) hit back on Tuesday, saying Saral’s “irresponsible” comments risked harming ties between the close allies.

Zahid Oruj, chairman of the human rights committee of the National Assembly, Azerbaijan’s parliament, said the measure was not an act of religious discrimination or an attack on free expression.

“There is no ban on wearing headscarves outside school, and the primary objective is to maintain uniform rules within the educational environment,” he told Al Jazeera.

He added that many Azerbaijanis do not wear the hijab but still regard the Quran as a holy book and believe in God, suggesting that disagreement about school dress requirements should not be equated with hostility towards religion.

The National NGO Forum of Azerbaijan has likewise criticised what it describes as the politicisation of the debate.

Azerbaijan’s secularism is enshrined in its constitution. Article 7 defines the country as a secular state. Article 18 establishes the separation of religion and state and provides for the secular character of the state education system. However, Article 48 guarantees freedom of conscience.

These provisions place secular education and religious freedom within the same constitutional framework, raising questions about how the state should reconcile them when regulating clothing in public schools.

Azer Rashidoglu, chairman of the Azerbaijan-based Tolerance Public Association for Social Research, believes the new rules are not in line with the Constitution and said people affected should challenge the measures.

“Those whose rights have been violated should collectively seek legal redress through the courts and pursue their cause through peaceful and lawful means,” he said.

articles.title: One man dead and two missing as search goes on for fishing boat off Lewis
articles.summary: The alarm was raised after the men's fishing boat failed to return as planned to Lewis.
articles.body:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised at about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat was overdue from Lewis.

A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers were making searches off the Port of Ness in north Lewis.

Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men.

Police Scotland said: "The body of one of the men has been recovered, however formal identification is yet to take place.

"The next of kin of the men are aware and are being supported by officers.

"Extensive searches, assisted by HM Coastguard and RNLI, are ongoing."

The RNLI said Stornoway's all-weather lifeboat was launched at 21:42 on Tuesday to search for the overdue fishing boat.

A spokesperson said: "The search, involving coastguard air and ground assets, was joined by Lochinver RNLI's all-weather lifeboat a short time later and continued into Wednesday morning."

Kenneth Macleod, convener of local authority Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, told BBC Radio Scotland's Lunchtime Live programme : "It is a very dark day for the community of Ness and the community of Lewis in general.

"Our thoughts and condolences are with the families affected.

"We cannot comprehend what the families of the three fishermen are going through at the moment."

Macleod said the search involved coastguard helicopters from Stornoway in Lewis and Shetland, as well as coastguard teams and local boats.

The search has come during warnings of bad weather in the area.

A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK.

A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places.

articles.title: How do Iranians move money abroad to avoid US sanctions?
articles.summary: From currency brokers to crypto, Iranians find ways to circumvent sanctions, but each comes with its own problems.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Decades of international sanctions have severely restricted Iran’s access to the global financial system, making cross-border payments difficult for individuals and businesses alike. The sanctions have only increased with the current US-Israeli war on Iran.

Unable to rely on conventional banking for international transactions, many Iranians have turned to alternative channels to pay for goods and services abroad.

And while each workaround channel offers a way to navigate some of the restrictions, it comes with its own costs and risks, often falling short of the security, reliability and efficiency of a functioning international banking system.

One alternative financial channel is relying on networks of currency exchangers that operate across borders, an informal system that matches those who need local currency in Iran with those who need foreign currency abroad. By balancing these opposing needs, transactions can be settled without money necessarily moving directly between Iranian and foreign bank accounts.

Intermediary firms offer services comparable to currency exchange traders. Typically, a customer pays the intermediary in local currency in Iran, while the firm or an overseas partner arranges payment to the foreign supplier in a convertible currency, using funds held abroad.

Using currency traders or intermediary firms can help bridge gaps in international banking access, but both often involve additional fees, exchange-rate costs, delays and greater complexity.

Other Iranians don’t deal with companies, but resort to private arrangements with individuals, including people they do not know personally, to transfer money across borders. Those deals may offer a practical solution when formal channels are unavailable, but they rely heavily on trust rather than enforceable guarantees.

“The transaction involves strangers having to trust one another to conduct a deal without any legal documentation or proof,” said Reza, an Iranian IT manager in Germany, who did not wish to give his full name. “It relies entirely on trust, and either party can back out at any time, leaving the others out of pocket.”

The methods used – whether through companies or individuals – are informal and not the most secure. “We have to use informal exchange and remittance systems for international trade, which carries risks such as lost funds, fraud and high transfer costs,” explained Ashkan Bahrami, an Iranian trade expert.

These networks are also vulnerable to geopolitical shocks. Some operating through Gulf countries have been disrupted by the war, adding another layer of uncertainty for businesses and individuals dependent on them.

Cryptocurrency has offered another route, enabling users to transfer wealth without relying on conventional banks. But even these digital assets have not provided a fully reliable escape from sanctions. Earlier this year, the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned several major Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges, including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin and Ramzinex.

Alireza Yaghoubi, chairman of Iran’s FinTech Association board, warned that crypto transactions are traceable, “and very bad things can happen, such as the sanctions imposed on multiple Iranian wallets, whether they belonged to individuals, the Central Bank, or other entities”.

The possibility of sanctions, combined with periodic internet disruptions, makes cryptocurrency an uncertain option.

For businesses importing physical goods, the challenges extend beyond payment itself. War-related disruptions and restrictions, particularly after the US naval blockade on Iran, have complicated transportation, lengthened delivery times, and increased uncertainty over when shipments will arrive.

Arghavan Ghazanfari, CEO of Aron Trading Group, described the scale of the disruption facing importers using the port of Shanghai in China, a major gateway for goods shipped to Iran.

“Transit time used to be 26 days. But when it stretches nowadays to 102 or even 120 days, customers are bound to reconsider importing,” Ghazanfari said. “Unfortunately, the main problem now is that our supply routes are gradually being cut off.”

And even when Iranians find a way to make payments abroad – and are willing to accept the delays in receiving their goods – another problem remains: whether they can afford what they are trying to buy.

The Iranian rial’s sustained depreciation has sharply eroded purchasing power. Against the US dollar, Iran’s currency has lost more than 10 percent of its value over the past month, more than 55 percent over the past year and almost 90 percent over the past five years.

And there is little certainty that the pressure will ease anytime soon.

With the prospect of another escalation in the conflict looming over Iran and uncertainty clouding the country’s economic outlook, the question for many Iranians is not simply how to move money across borders. It is how long they can keep navigating an increasingly restrictive financial system, and what it will cost them to do so.

articles.title: Trump says ‘massive’ oil, gas and mineral exploration to begin in Greenland
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland” early Wednesday.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland” early Wednesday. It wasn’t immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States. Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska, to stump for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan as he seeks his third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former U.S. congresswoman Mary Peltola. Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump’s war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America’s working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before they head to the polls. But despite Trump’s optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island’s harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage. Trump’s comments about the Arctic island come less than a month after he signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president’s repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It does not grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors. The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence. Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally. Representatives of the leaders of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday. Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world’s supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing’s chokehold on them. The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas. But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice. Trump’s Truth Social post also touted Greenland’s strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe,” the island is “second to none.” “Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he wrote. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!” The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO. Trump said last month that the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”

articles.title: The Gentlemen star Ray Winstone charms locals in Cowbridge
articles.summary: Winstone plays Alan "Razor" Sharp, an ex-SAS operative, in the action comedy Danger Money.
articles.body:
An actor renowned for his "hard man" image and London gangster roles looked at home filming on the more genteel streets of a south Wales market town.

Ray Winstone, recently seen in Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen, as well as star of The Departed and Sexy Beast, was spotted in Cowbridge in the Vale of Glamorgan, filming the six-part action-comedy Danger Money.

Winstone leads the cast as Alan "Razor" Sharp, an ex-SAS operative, with Cowbridge portraying a town in England.

"It created a real buzz," said Nadine Price, supervisor at Ground coffee shop on High Street, one of the filming locations.

Price said there was "real excitement" in the town, with Winstone spending time joking with residents.

The Welsh flag was taken down from the town hall for the filming, with Price saying Cowbridge would be depicted as a town in Herefordshire.

Winstone, 69, who was born in east London and is famous for his Cockney accent, walked the high street of Cowbridge wearing military medals and a flat cap in character as Sharp.

Winstone previously said his character was "a bit of a scrapper, surly and getting on a bit".

"I told them it doesn't ring any bells, but I like a challenge," he joked.

Molly Ridge, a stylist at Minnie May Closet, was about to film a promotional Instagram reel for the shop when she noticed the filming outside.

"I had one of our dresses on so I ran up to him and asked him for a selfie and he said 'yes of course babes, that's fine babes'. He was just really sweet.

"He said the dress looked gorgeous and I thought he could have been a bit off as he was just about to start filming but he wasn't."

She described Winstone as a "lovely man" who was "exactly the same in character as in real life with his proper gruff East End accent".

Anna Groom also works at the shop and asked for an autograph.

"He signed it to the 'Lovely Anna' which I thought was sweet and he came across like a really nice guy," she said.

Gary Simms, a Cowbridge local, also had a picture with the actor when he saw him in the Bear Hotel on Sunday evening, the night before filming.

"What a nice guy. We were watching [the] Liverpool-Man City game and we had a great chat about football, and he was wearing his West Ham joggers.

"It was surreal to see him in the pub as I'd just finished watching season two of The Gentlemen."

Winstone also recently appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, where his daughter, Jaime, is a contestant, sending a video message of support after she was in the dance off.

articles.title: Singapore pollution spikes and East Timor shuts schools as Indonesia wildfire haze intensifies
articles.summary: Pollution readings in Singapore reached their highest level this year on Wednesday while East Timor shut its schools for three days in response to intensifying smoke and haze from Indonesia’s wildfires.
articles.body: Pollution readings in Singapore reached their highest level this year on Wednesday while East Timor shut its schools for three days in response to intensifying smoke and haze from Indonesia’s wildfires. Singapore’s one-hour PM2.5 reading hit a high of 284 micrograms per cubic meter in the western part of the island state, entering the National Environmental Agency’s “very high” band for the first time during the current haze period. The East Timor government said in a statement that it was suspending face-to-face learning activities for three days starting Thursday “due to contamination by pollutant particles from wildfires in neighboring regions or countries.” East Timor did not identify Indonesia by name, but it shares an island with a part of Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province, where a number of hotspots have been reported. Indonesia has been battling its most intense wildfire season in 11 years, fueled by El Niño-related dry weather conditions. The haze has caused a spike in respiratory illnesses at home and a dramatic decline in air quality across the region, with several states in Malaysia also forced to shut down schools. In October 2015, Indonesian wildfires brought PM2.5 levels in the west of Singapore up to a national record of 471 micrograms per cubic meter. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has ordered additional resources to be deployed to combat the wildfires. “We are mobilizing all our resources and capabilities,” Honi Havana, an official at the Coordinating Ministry for Political and Security Affairs, said at a Wednesday news briefing. He said Jakarta had deployed more than 69,000 firefighting personnel, up from around 44,000 in mid-September, and that it was also testing new methods to put out fires more effectively using special chemicals. Authorities have been struggling with peatland fires, which smolder slowly beneath the surface and can re-emerge anytime, said disaster mitigation agency spokesperson Berton Panjaitan. “We must recognize that the only way to resolve this is through sustained rainfall,” he said. As Southeast Asian foreign ministers prepare to discuss the issue of transboundary haze at an ASEAN meeting next month, criticism of Indonesia has continued to mount across the region. On Tuesday, Malaysian lawmaker Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman called on Southeast Asian nations to lodge a diplomatic protest against Jakarta for failing to do enough to control the fires. “We must send a strong diplomatic note that Malaysia objects, and that not only Malaysia objects, it must be agreed upon by other ASEAN countries that are similarly affected, such as Singapore. We must send a very clear diplomatic protest,” he told parliament. “You need to treat them like an outcast in the region,” he said, adding that Malaysian and Singaporean banks should cut off financing to companies linked to land burning.

articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella 'remembers' the review of an acquisition he sat through with Bill Gates that still haunts him; says: I got out of the meeting thinking ...
articles.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently recalled a meeting with Bill Gates that still continues to haunt him.
articles.body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently recalled a meeting with Bill Gates that still continues to haunt him. Speaking on the Confession with Ali Partovi podcast, Satya Nadella described a meeting from around 2008 or 2009, when he was running the business that would later become Bing. The meeting concerned an acquisition being considered by Microsoft's enterprise business. Nadella said that the meeting still ‘haunts’ him bn not because of the acquisition being discussed, but because he failed to speak up against a decision he believed was fundamentally flawed.“I remember another more consequential meeting. This was maybe 2008, 2009 maybe. Bill called a meeting. I was at that time running what became Bing later on. And this was an acquisition our enterprise business was making”, Satya Nadella said.He further explained that the proposed deal involved a team working on parallel data warehousing, an area where he felt the company's approach was heading in the wrong direction. “And they were trying to buy some kind of a parallel data warehouse team. I looked at it. It is completely architecturally stupid in that time to go buy that. This is this other team sort of making some decision which made no sense.”Why the meeting with Bill Gates still haunts Satya NadellaSatya Nadella's regret was not limited to his disagreement with the proposed acquisition. He said the experience made him think about how people in important meetings can fail to speak up even when they believe they see a problem that others may have missed. During the podcast, he recalled leaving the meeting without challenging the decision."I sat in this review. I distinctly remember this. In fact, it haunts me to think that I may be in a review where there's somebody in that meeting who sees the future a lot more clearly than I do and the other person presenting, but does not really advocate for it. articles.title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
articles.summary: The Competition and Markets Authority has fined Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym £6m in total.
articles.body:
Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds.

The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said.

Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships.

It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate.

Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment.

Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA.

The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds.

Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March.

The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added.

The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%.

Eight firms under investigation over online pricing

AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees

A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers".

Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead.

Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics.

"When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added.

Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics.

"Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines."

Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response.

"The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said.

The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways.

Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers.

However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.

Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines.

Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said.

articles.title: Meet Daniil Prokofev, the 17-year-old Virginia student who helped build a safer walking app; 14 schools are now piloting the program
articles.summary: For most students, getting home from school is a routine journey. For Daniil Prokofev, an eight-mile run home turned into something far more consequential.
articles.body: For most students, getting home from school is a routine journey. For Daniil Prokofev, an eight-mile run home turned into something far more consequential. A route generated by Google Maps sent the 17-year-old along a stretch of Braddock Road without sidewalks, forcing him close to traffic and through shrubbery as daylight faded. What should have been a straightforward trip quickly became a lesson in how navigation apps can overlook one crucial factor: whether a route is actually safe for the person using it. That experience eventually led Prokofev and two classmates at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Alexandria, Virginia, to create SafeWalkr, a walking navigation platform designed with student safety in mind. The project, which began as a 24-hour coding challenge, is now being piloted across 14 Fairfax County Public Schools, states an online report by FCPS News.When the fastest route isn't the safestProkofev, now a senior, had assumed that a standard pedestrian route would account for basic safety. Instead, his experience highlighted a gap shared by many walkers and cyclists. Conventional navigation systems tend to focus heavily on reaching a destination quickly, but the shortest route can sometimes mean walking beside fast-moving traffic, crossing roads with limited pedestrian infrastructure or reaching stretches without sidewalks, states the online report.When Prokofev discussed the problem with fellow TJHSST seniors Ashwath Muppa and Isaac Leetyn, they discovered they had encountered similar issues. The three students began considering whether technology could be used to make pedestrian navigation more useful for children travelling to and from school. Their opportunity arrived during HackTJ, the school's annual coding competition, adds the report by FCPS News.Building a smarter walking routeDrawing on skills developed in a machine learning class taught by TJHSST teacher Nicole Kim, the students began developing an algorithm that could weigh safety alongside travel time. The resulting SafeWalkr platform combines information from Fairfax County records, Google Maps imagery and street databases. The system maps details such as crosswalks, traffic volumes and sidewalk coverage, allowing its algorithm to identify routes that offer a better balance between convenience and pedestrian safety.According to FCPS News, the students used Python, JavaScript and C++ to build the system and developed a mobile-friendly website intended for both parents and students. The premise was relatively simple: much of the information needed to identify safer routes already exists, but it is not necessarily incorporated into mainstream navigation algorithms.From hackathon to school pilotSafeWalkr might have remained a winning hackathon concept if not for the support it received from school officials. TJHSST Principal Mike Mukai encouraged the students to connect with Fairfax County Public Schools' Safe Routes to School team, introducing them to Becky Gray. The collaboration helped the students refine the platform around the practical needs of families. They also consulted FCPS Chief Technology Officer Gautam Sethi on cybersecurity and web-hosting requirements, while Chief Safety and Security Officer Brian Lambert helped them consider operational safety protocols.TJHSST math teacher Sewon Yang served as the project's advisor, helping the students pursue funding and offering feedback alongside Mukai as the platform developed.14 schools join the programmeThe report also states that SafeWalkr will be piloted for families living within the walking zones of 14 FCPS schools, with the launch timed to coincide with National Walk and Roll to School Day. The participating elementary schools are Annandale Terrace, Bush Hill, Cardinal Forest, Chesterbrook, Freedom Hill, Lemon Road, Kings Park, Ravensworth, McNair and Mt. Eagle. Cooper and Twain are the participating middle schools, while Hayfield Secondary and Justice High round out the secondary and high-school participants.Image Courtesy: FCPS NewsYou use AI every day. articles.title: How a radio glitch triggered a false hijack alert in Germany
articles.summary: Authorities scrambled fighter jets to escort a plane from Corfu to Nuremberg after a pilot sent a hijack alert.
articles.body:
German authorities briefly closed an airport and scrambled fighter jets to escort a passenger plane on Tuesday following an emergency alert indicating a hijacking was taking place on board. However, the alert had been accidentally triggered by a radio “malfunction”.

Corendon Airlines said its Boeing 737-800, which was en route from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to Nuremberg, Germany, sent out an emergency code while it was flying over Croatia “due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system”.

In a statement, the airline said that “no emergency situation occurred”, and the 178 passengers, flight crew and aircraft had not been in danger at any point. The plane landed safely in Nuremberg.

German police said Corendon Airlines flight XR456 “inadvertently” sent out an emergency “squawk” alert with the code 7500 while flying over Croatia on Tuesday.

A squawk is a four-digit code a pilot sends via the jet’s transponder to air traffic control. The code 7500 tells air traffic controllers that a hijacking is in progress.

However, air traffic controllers were unable to make contact with the pilots or crew, causing the alarm to be raised further. It is unclear why this happened.

“The aircraft could no longer be reached by radio to clarify the situation”, prompting warnings to be activated in several European countries, police said.

A Rafale fighter jet was scrambled from Croatia to intercept the Boeing passenger jet, while the German military also dispatched warplanes.

Police cordoned off the Albrecht Dürer airport in Nuremberg as a precaution until they knew the reason the pilot had sent the hijack alert.

Police spokesman Michael Petzold explained that authorities had “received a code directly from the cockpit that suggested a hijacking”.

“Since we were then unable to reach the cockpit, and the tower was also unable to contact the cockpit, we had to assume the worst – that it might indeed be a hijacking,” Petzold said.

The incident disrupted flights, with six flights delayed and two inbound flights diverted to other airports as a precaution, a Nuremberg airport spokesperson said.

Why are aviation authorities so concerned?

The hijack scare has come amid heightened concerns about aviation security after the copilot on board a Flydubai jet bound for Israel from Dubai attacked the captain with an emergency crash axe, forcing the flight to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on September 30.

On Friday, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said the copilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv and called the incident a “terrorist attack”.

Also, before the false hijack alert in the early hours of Tuesday, flights had been briefly disrupted at Nuremberg ‌airport after pilots reported suspected drone sightings.

Authorities across Europe have already stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks after a series of mostly mysterious drone incidents and concerns about Russian hybrid warfare.

Western nations, including Germany, have accused Moscow of launching a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disruption to undermine European support for Ukraine and destabilise the continent.

Several German airports have had to suspend operations for brief periods in recent months due to drone activity, with suspicion often falling on Russia.

Last month, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August using a drone laden with explosives. Berlin closed the Russian consulate among other measures.

Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin “fabricated” the evidence. However, in light of the concerns, NATO’s top general told the Warsaw Security Forum earlier this week that the alliance has a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on its members, embedding lessons learned from the Ukrainian front lines.

How common are radio glitches and false hijack alerts?

Radio glitches are common, but incidents rarely escalate to major security events because pilots use back-up radios to communicate with air traffic controllers when they lose communication signals.

In 2019, a pilot flying an Air Europa jet from Amsterdam to Madrid accidentally transmitted hijack alert 7500. For half an hour, aviation authorities thought the alarm was a genuine emergency and followed safety protocols, which disrupted flights and led to the evacuation of part of Schipol airport in the Netherlands.

In 2011, a flight from Chicago to Germany was diverted to Toronto when a pilot spilled coffee and accidentally set off a hijack alarm. The spill caused distress signals to go out, including the 7500 transponder code.

articles.title: Trump rejects international election monitors, breaking 2-decade tradition
articles.summary: President Trump is breaking a more than two-decade-long tradition of welcoming a key group of international election observers to monitor the midterm contest, drawing criticism for discouraging democratic transparency. The U.S. has routinely invited election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to observe and report on midterm and presidential contests…
articles.body:
President Trump is breaking a more than two-decade-long tradition of welcoming a key group of international election observers to monitor the midterm contest, drawing criticism for discouraging democratic transparency.

The U.S. has routinely invited election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to observe and report on midterm and presidential contests since 2002. Election observations are carried out by the OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR).

Trump’s decision puts the U.S. in the same basket as the isolated, autocratic regimes of Belarus and Russia. Those countries have also rejected international observers, and their most recent elections were widely condemned as a sham.

The U.S. is one of the 57 members of the OSCE, an international body created after the Cold War to promote democracy and human rights in post-Soviet states. The U.S. hosting OSCE election observers is viewed as an important signal of transparency that encourages countries with more vulnerable democracies to open up their elections to observation and monitoring.

“The Trump Administration’s decision not to invite international observers to the United States is deeply antithetical to the spirit of freedom, democracy and transparency that defines our elections,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the outgoing ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement.

“I urge the Trump Administration to respect the role of independent election observers and ensure that the United States holds itself to the same standards that we would expect of any other democracy.”

Shaheen is also a member of the Helsinki Commission, an independent organization led by members of Congress and housed on Capitol Hill that monitors OSCE compliance in member states.

The election-monitoring mission of the OSCE’s human rights office, the ODIHR, does not have any enforcement mechanisms, and it does not determine whether an election is legitimate. Its purpose is to assess the election environment and make recommendations to bring it more in line with OSCE commitments on democratic standards.

“No other nation has done more to advance the cause of human freedom and representative government. American elections will be administered, participated in, and observed by American citizens,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in response to a question about why the Trump administration withheld an invitation to the OSCE.

The Trump administration’s decision is “regrettable,” the ODIHR and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly said in a statement last month .

“After more than two decades in which the United States has welcomed OSCE observers to its federal elections, this decision represents a significant departure from an established democratic practice,” Pere Joan Pons, president of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, said.

Despite its long history, the OSCE election-monitoring mission is a little obscure even among lawmakers and staff on Capitol Hill.

But the fact that the Trump administration knew of the practice and made a point to block election monitors is a red flag, said Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.), the House’s ranking member on the Helsinki Commission.

“I think Trump doesn’t want any observers at all because I think he’s got some hijinks that he’s going to lay on the nation on Election Day,” Cohen, who is retiring from Congress at the end of this term after his seat was redistricted, told The Hill.

“I think this is a tip, when you say you don’t want the OSCE observers, that means there’s something you don’t want to observe.”

Likewise, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), the Senate’s ranking member on the Helsinki Commission, called the absence of OSCE observers a “warning sign for democracy” in a statement to The Hill.

“The OSCE has been observing American elections for over twenty years, and has been welcomed by administrations of both parties, including Trump 1.0,” he said.

“Booting the OSCE monitors is a warning sign for democracy that puts the U.S. in the company of Russia and Belarus.”

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.), the chair and co-chair of the Helsinki Commission, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Trump’s critics are concerned that the president is laying the groundwork to disrupt or dispute election returns that don’t favor Republican candidates, in the same vein of his rejection of his 2020 election loss to former President Biden.

“A defining characteristic of a strong, secure democracy is its willingness to subject its electoral processes to independent scrutiny,” read a statement from the Democracy Renewal Group.

The organization was founded by about 200 former U.S. Agency for International Development staff members, who were purged with the Trump administration’s gutting of the agency, and other democracy and governance professionals and consultants.

Democracy Renewal Group condemned the exclusion of election monitors.

“If this decision stands, the United States will join a notorious group of countries too threatened by independent scrutiny to invite observers: Russia, Belarus, and Yugoslavia under Slobodan Milosevic in 2000,” the group wrote.

State officials, mostly Democrats, are preparing for and thinking about any way the Trump administration could try to assert federal control over state-administered elections, according to a report on VoteBeat.org , a nonpartisan news site reporting on elections and voting. Their concerns include the possibility of immigration officers being dispatched to polling stations and federal attempts to seize ballots.

The Supreme Court’s decision last month to block Trump from implementing an executive order widely criticized as restricting Americans’ access to mail-in voting was celebrated by voting rights advocates and Democrats.

Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.), a member of the Committee on House Administration, which has oversight of federal elections, said he is talking with election officials about preparing to challenge any attempts by the Trump administration to disenfranchise American voters.

“I don’t want to overreact to the president, but yes, we are doing draft pleadings,” he said in an interview with MS NOW.

“We’re talking to lawyers all over this country. We’re prepared, but people should have confidence and should go out and vote.”

articles.title: Hooters restaurants keep closing even as CEO says there's more to the story
articles.summary: Hooters CEO Neil Kiefer told Fox News Digital that recent restaurant closures aren't a sign of brand weakness as the original founders rebuild after its 2025 bankruptcy.
articles.body: Hooters restaurants continue to disappear across America, including several longtime locations in Florida — but the iconic chain's CEO insists the closures aren't a sign that the brand is losing its appeal. Neil Kiefer, CEO of Florida-based Hooters Inc., told Fox News Digital the company is focused on rebuilding the restaurant chain after its original founders regained control of the brand following its 2025 bankruptcy. "The number of stores will go up and down, but the longevity of our commitment will not," Kiefer said. "These store closures are not an indication of brand strength." HOOTERS RESTAURANTS KEEP DISAPPEARING AS ICONIC CHAIN LOSES LONGTIME LOCATIONS IN FOUNDING STATE His remarks come after Fox News Digital reported that Hooters closed its last remaining restaurant in Jacksonville, Florida, ending a 40-year presence in the city. The closure followed the September shutdown of a Hooters in Panama City Beach, which had operated for more than three decades. Other longtime locations have also disappeared, including a Hooters in Boca Raton, Florida, which closed earlier this year after 16 years when its landlord declined to renew the lease. But Kiefer said the recent closures need to be viewed in the context of the company's ownership changes. "In March 2025, Hooters of America filed for bankruptcy," he said. HISTORY OF HOOTERS: 5 FACTS YOU LIKELY NEVER KNEW ABOUT THE RESTAURANT CHAIN "Hooters of America was a separate corporate entity from the original Hooters team that first founded the brand and their first restaurant in Clearwater, Florida, in 1983," he went on. "While these two groups may have shared a name, they shared nothing else. The original founders saw an opportunity to step in and reclaim their brand, integrity and legacy. Since these acquisitions, we've learned some stores were in various stages of need." Kiefer also emphasized that the closures should not be viewed as a reflection of the restaurant chain's "beloved staff, community or sisterhood of the orange shorts." The restaurant chain has been working to reinvent itself under its new ownership — with a renewed emphasis on food, hospitality and attracting families. That strategy has included opening new restaurants, including a location in The Villages, Florida, in July 2025, while another location in Lutz, near Tampa, is coming soon, according to its website. The Villages restaurant has also attracted attention for its popularity among retirees, demonstrating how the brand is attempting to appeal to a broader customer base. Following the Jacksonville and Boca Raton closures, large stretches of the state's Atlantic coast are without a Hooters restaurant. articles.title: Israeli air strike kills Palestinian woman in Gaza City
articles.summary: The woman’s young daughter was rescued from a large fire inside the apartment, caused by the attack.
articles.body:
An Israeli air strike on an apartment block in Gaza has killed a woman and wounded two other people, hospital officials said.

Reem Asaad Awad, 33, was killed in the attack early on Wednesday in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City, the Turkish state news agency Anadolu reported, quoting a source at Al Shifa hospital.

The source said the strike caused extensive destruction to the targeted apartment and nearby buildings.

The daughter of the woman who was killed was rescued from a large fire that broke out after the attack.

Israel says it is investigating the strike and claims it targeted a member of Hamas, without providing evidence.

Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said the strike happened at 4am (01:00 GMT).

Israel has killed 1,501 Palestinians in Gaza since it agreed a “ceasefire” with the Palestinian group Hamas last October. The truce was part of a wider United States-backed proposal to end Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza.

Talks aimed at advancing to the second phase of the US plan, which includes the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas, have stalled.

The agreement states that 600 trucks of humanitarian aid are to be allowed into Gaza each day, but Israeli authorities have continued to impose severe restrictions on supplies entering the enclave, and reconstruction of the war-shattered territory has not begun.

articles.title: Maidstone fan not guilty of assault after fall from Ipswich stand
articles.summary: Away fan John Ryan toppled from the upper tier at Ipswich's ground and landed on home supporters.
articles.body:
A man who fell from the upper tier of a stand during a football match and injured fans below has been found not guilty of assault.

Maidstone United supporter John Ryan fell on to Joanne Peters and her partner Aaron Rose at Ipswich Town's Portman Road ground during an FA Cup clash in January 2024.

Ryan, 62, of Railway Street, Chatham, Kent, denied one count of assault by beating and one count of actual bodily harm and told Ipswich Crown Court he had been unable to stop himself during goal celebrations.

Ryan could be seen crying in the dock as the jury returned verdicts of not guilty to both charges and said afterwards "it's been very stressful".

Peters had been in tears when she told the court she initially thought the supporters' box behind her had collapsed and she thought she "could have died" .

Ryan had been one of thousands of Maidstone United supporters who saw their non-league side win 2-1 over Ipswich , who were heading to promotion from the Championship that season.

He told the court the game had been "the biggest match in the club's history" and he had been celebrating a "special" goal.

The jury was told he had been in Cobbold Stand upper tier when he fell, slid down the sloping roof that covers the boxes, and landed on the Ipswich supporters below.

Ryan told the jury he had been unsure if he had been pushed or his foot had slipped when he fell.

Prosecutor Simon Gladwell previously told the trial Ryan had drunk five cans of lager ahead of the match.

Peters said she had suffered "elements of whiplash" as well as numbness in her hands and internal bruising, while Rose told the jury he had been kicked in the head.

Rose believed Ryan had been drunk and told the trial "it wouldn't take a scientist to work it out".

Two years after the incident, Ryan was back in Ipswich for his trial at the crown court, which is just across the road from the stadium's Sir Alf Ramsey stand.

Shortly after Ryan's fall, Ipswich Town introduced glass screens at the bottom of the upper tier of the Cobbold Stand to try to improve safety.

Speaking to reporters outside court, Ryan said: "When you score a goal like that the last thing on your mind is what's going to happen.

"I just remember going down the stairs and I hit that barrier, fell over it and that was it."

Asked if he would like to say anything to Peters and Rose, Ryan said: "I'm sorry, it was an accident.

"I'm sorry it happened, what more can I say?"

Last month, Ryan was sentenced at Maidstone Magistrates' Court along with two other men for assaulting a man at Halling railway station in Kent.

He was given a three-year order banning him from any football ground in the UK, along with a community order, British Transport Police said .

articles.title: Hijack code 7500 appeared, pilots said all normal: The mystery behind Air India's Frankfurt-Delhi flight scare
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: What led to a false hijack scare that sent Air India’s longhaul Frankfurt-Delhi flight being diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday has now become the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: What led to a false hijack scare that sent Air India’s longhaul Frankfurt-Delhi flight being diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday has now become the subject of a probe by both aviation and security agencies. The Boeing 787-9 with about 300 people on board had entered Indian airspace via the long route taken these days due to closure of Pakistan skies for Indian carriers when Mumbai air traffic control systems received this aircraft squawking transponder code 7500 which is the aviation code for hijacking or unlawful interference.People in the know say the pilots denied squawking the code and they told ATC that everything was alright. But as per established protocol, the aircraft was diverted to Jaipur where it was parked on a remote bay. Extensive checks were carried out of everyone on board, baggage and the aircraft. Everything was found alright and the plane was cleared to take off for Delhi with the same crew operating this leg of the extended journey.“After Mumbai ATC received the aircraft squawking the code 7500, they spoke to the pilots who reported that all operations were normal on the flight. But protocols have to be followed in situations like which was done. Now it is being seen how and why this happened? Was there software on the ATC side?” said people in the know.Senior B787 pilots say there is a “one in a trillion” chance of the code being set to 7500 on the aircraft inadvertently or due to some error. “Each digit has to be physically entered. There is no button that can be inadvertently pressed. So from the pilot or plane side some error to happen is highly remote,” they say.Senior air traffic controllers say Mumbai ATC has a new system and that it’s “unlikely” to be a case of software error. “When a pilot squawks 7500 (hijack), then the colour of this aircraft’s dot on the radar screen turns red and an alarm goes off. Code 7600 is for emergency and 7700 for communication failure,” said an official.In a statement, Air India said: “Air India flight AI2030 operating from Frankfurt to Delhi on Oct 14 was diverted to Jaipur following a perceived security concern. The aircraft landed safely in Jaipur. The relevant security agencies carried out the necessary checks and have cleared the aircraft and crew. All passengers disembarked, underwent security checks, and have since reboarded the aircraft. The flight is expected to continue its journey to Delhi shortly.”“Air India teams worked proactively with authorities to minimise passenger inconvenience. We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused to our passengers due to this unforeseen disruption and appreciate their patience and understanding. The safety and security of our passengers and crew remain Air India's highest priority," AI statement added.After landing, the aircraft was escorted to an isolation bay, where a multi-agency security operation was launched. Teams from the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), local police and the Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) inspected the aircraft, passenger baggage and cargo holds.Police sources said security personnel conducted checks as part of the response. The National Security Guard (NSG) was also placed on standby in New Delhi, according to the information provided.Jaipur airport management said the passengers were taken to the terminal building after security checks. “The passengers have arrived in the terminal building. All are safe, and there is no situation of panic. The passengers are in the terminal building, and the authorities are now working on the plan for their departure to New Delhi,” airport sources told PTI.Airport authorities said normal flight movements and terminal operations continued during the security response. After the checks were completed, the Aerodrome Committee assessed the situation and concluded that the threat alert had been resolved. The aircraft and crew were then cleared for departure.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Russia’s arrest of Japanese journalist: Why are tensions rising?
articles.summary: Japanese journalist Imai Yuki arrested on Sakhalin for allegedly spying on Russian defence capabilities, says the FSB.
articles.body:
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist from Sakhalin Island after accusing him of spying and gathering information on its defence capabilities.

On Tuesday, Russian news agencies reported that the reporter, working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was arrested by the Federal Security Service (FSB) as he was preparing to leave the next day.

According to the TASS news agency, the FSB said the journalist, Imai Yuki, was arrested in the Sakhalin region and taken to Moscow after being accused in a “criminal case”.

The arrest of the Japanese citizen comes amid deteriorating relations between the two countries as Tokyo joined Western sanctions against Moscow due to the invasion of Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s August visit to Iturup Island, which is part of the Kuril Islands archipelago, drew sharp reactions from Japan.

The two countries have a longstanding territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands dating back more than a century.

Who is the arrested journalist and what is he accused of?

Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova, during a press briefing on Tuesday, said Yuki was accused of espionage.

“Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country’s security are regrettable. We cannot help but point out that today’s incident is not an isolated one,” Zakharova said.

“Given the overall decline in bilateral cooperation caused by the Japanese authorities’ anti-Russian policies since the start of the Second World War, as well as Tokyo’s reluctance to listen to Moscow’s concerns regarding Japan’s remilitarisation policy, which affects our legitimate security interests in the Far East, we are forced to note that this development will further darken the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations.”

Zakharova called on Tokyo to “come to its senses and change its approach, abandoning hostile steps towards Russia”.

According to Russia’s Interfax news agency, Yuki will be remanded until December 12 before the trial begins.

On Wednesday morning, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo had requested the “prompt provision of information” from Russian authorities over the arrest.

“As well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” he added.

Japanese media have also reported that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs would summon the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a protest over the arrest, but no official confirmation has been released so far.

The Hokkaido Shimbun, where Yuki worked, said it was still confirming details and added that it would “respond with the reporter’s safety as our top priority”.

What’s the history of Russia-Japan tensions over Sakhalin Island?

While Russia administers the Kuril Islands archipelago, Japan claims the four southernmost islands – Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets – calling them the Northern Territories.

The Kuril chain of islands sits between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.

The dispute began in 1855, after Russia and Japan established their first diplomatic and trade treaty, which also drew the Russo-Japanese border in the Kuril Islands, with Iturup under Japanese control and the islands to the north under Russian control.

Russia took control of the Kuril Islands after the 1945 Yalta agreement, which was signed by United States President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

Following Japan’s surrender in the final weeks of World War II, Moscow seized the entire archipelago and expelled about 17,000 Japanese citizens.

In the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty, Japan renounced the Kurils but maintained that the four southernmost islands were part of its territory. However, Russia never signed the treaty.

Because of the ongoing dispute, Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty to end World War II.

What’s behind the recent rise in tensions?

In August, Putin visited Iturup on his first-ever trip to the disputed islands.

He was the second president to visit the islands after his predecessor, Dmitry Medvedev.

But Putin’s visit caused uproar, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling it “absolutely unacceptable”.

Takaichi told reporters at the time that Putin’s visit had “worsened Japanese sentiment towards Russia”, adding that the chain of islands was a “unique territory of [Japan] historically and under international law”.

“I hope that the Russian side will take the gravity of this matter very seriously,” she said.

Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also said the islands were “inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit”.

What is the status of Russia-Japan relations?

Relations between the two neighbouring countries are at a low point.

Russia has increased its military presence on the Kuril Islands over the past decade, with Iturup used as its primary military airbase in the region.

Moscow has also labelled Japan as an “unfriendly” country due to sanctions over the Ukraine war.

On the other hand, Takaichi’s cabinet last week approved additional sanctions against Moscow, including expanded export bans and asset freezes for those linked to the Russian military.

articles.title: Settlers set fire to mosque in West Bank as Israeli forces raid villages
articles.summary: Settlers also attacked a boy in a separate incident in the town of Beita, south of Nablus.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have set fire to a mosque, an olive tree and a vehicle in the occupied West Bank, as Israeli forces continue to carry out raids across the territory.

The settlers started the fires while raiding the village of Mikhmas early on Wednesday, according to the Palestinian news agency, Wafa.

Reports online say the settlers spray painted racist slogans on the walls of the mosque, as well as other buildings and Palestinians’ homes.

Pogroms carried out by settlers across the occupied Palestinian territory have surged since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have accused the Israeli government of facilitating settler violence in a push to expand Israeli control of Palestinian land.

Elsewhere in the West Bank on Wednesday, settlers attacked a Palestinian boy in the town of Beita, south of Nablus, while Israeli forces arrested three Palestinians following a raid in the city of Qalqilya. Troops also raided the village of Tammun and fired tear gas, according to the Palestinian news outlet Quds News Network.

With the olive harvest under way across the West Bank, Israeli settlers have been mobilising to intimidate and obstruct Palestinian farmers, who rely on the crop as a crucial source of revenue.

According to Amnesty International, about 750,000 settlers live illegally in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.

articles.title: Thousands of refrigerators were hacked across France. How worried should you be?
articles.summary: Supermarket staffers were confronted by pools of water beneath freezers and spoiled produce earlier this week after hackers took control of refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France.
articles.body: Supermarket staffers were confronted by pools of water beneath freezers and spoiled produce earlier this week after hackers took control of refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France. Around 700 food retailers were impacted by the nationwide cyberattack, in which hackers remotely connected to refrigeration equipment, switched on defrost cycles that led to the loss of large quantities of fresh and frozen goods, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV. French authorities have opened an investigation into what the country’s Economy Minister Roland Lescure called a “wake-up call for everyone” in an address to lawmakers on Tuesday. Here’s what you need to know. Who caused the hack? No group or individual has yet claimed responsibility for the cyberattack. The fact that hackers have not publicly demanded a ransom – as is often the case – suggests their primary aim was little more than to cause “mischief,” or “unsettle the public,” Ken Munro, a UK-based cybersecurity analyst, told CNN. The hackers’ motivation is “unknown at this stage,” said Félix Aimé, principal threat researcher at French cybersecurity firm Sekoia. “To our knowledge, no public claim of responsibility has been made,” added Aimé, who previously worked at ANSSI, the French national cyber agency that is now handling the investigation. The possibility that a lone hacker or hacktivist group carried out the attack cannot be ruled out, Aimé said. “An operation intended to destabilize certain economic activities, or infrastructure could also be considered,” he told CNN. Moreover, the perpetrators do not appear to have used malicious code on the fridge controllers, potentially complicating efforts to track down who carried out the cyberattack, added Aimé. The Paris prosecutors’ office said it took up the case under its national jurisdiction into the “large-scale cyberattack affecting the connected refrigerators of several major food retailers across France,” in a statement to CNN on Tuesday. The investigation will “identify the victims and establish the link between the attacks and the damage they reported, in terms of food spoilage and fires,” the statement added. How did the attack happen? Fridge and freezer aisles in grocery stores are operated by controllers that can be accessed online, allowing maintenance firms to adjust the temperature remotely. In France, hackers penetrated controllers run by at least three firms – including the Danish company, Danfoss, the US-based company, Copeland and Dixell – according to a statement to CNN from ANSSI. Shortly after the cyberattack, Danfoss acknowledged that many of the impacted units “no longer receive software or security updates” or were “running outdated software.” The company urged customers to “keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware.” Copeland, which owns Dixell, identified a “vulnerability” in a “discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers.” “We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company told CNN in a statement. CNN has reached out to Danfoss for comment. The Danish firm, or the fridge installers, may have erroneously put the controllers on the public internet “for anyone to see,” said Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity organization, Pen Test Partners. Before the cyberattack, more than 1,700 instances of the affected Danfoss software were exposed to the internet in France, offering the hackers a broad potential target pool, said Aimé. Earlier this year, the cybersecurity company Claroty pointed out vulnerabilities in the controllers at the center of the attack – Danfoss AK-SM 800A – citing a mechanism that “could be abused” to “bypass normal authentication,” in a report published early August. That vulnerability can allow an attacker to remotely change the temperature settings for fridges running the affected software, added Aimé. By tapping into units’ built-in defrost function and removing limits that would usually prevent the temperature from rising, perpetrators caused the refrigerators to thaw overnight, according to UK Cyber Defence, a security analysis firm. Display cabinets peaked at 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for around six hours overnight Monday, with some even catching fire. “It wasn’t hard to work out how to take control of the fridges,” said Munro, adding that unit management at these retailers was likely “outsourced to a third party who gave little to no thought to maintaining the security of these fridges.” How widespread is the problem? Major supermarket groups in France were hit by the attack, prompting warnings from retail executives that the cost of the damage could run into the millions. As many as 80 supermarkets belonging to the French brand Carrefour were impacted, as were 5% of Monoprix’s 490 stores. Retail group Les Mousquetaires, reported that fridges at 150 shops had been targeted. About 80 Coopérative U stores were also affected, said its CEO, Dominique Schelcher. And the issue does not appear contained within France. Aimé told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected by the attack. How concerned should consumers be? For consumers, there is not a lot to be concerned about, said Munro. However, he cautioned that management systems for the fridges involved must be “kept off the public internet” with validated security. “There was no business need for the fridge controllers to be accessible on the public internet,” he said. “What I do recommend is that the boards of businesses ask probing questions of their suppliers. Who outsourced the management of these fridges and who had contractual oversight for their security? It doesn’t take much for one blind spot in a business to lead to tonnes of trashed food.” The attack sparked a wave of criticism from European officials, just weeks after French President Emmanuel Macron instructed lawmakers to draft a new protection plan against the growing threat of cyberattacks in the country, and beyond. Speaking to reporters after a meeting in Paris with political party leaders in September, Macron cited the “Russian hybrid threat facing Europeans and France,” adding that the risk had “intensified” in recent weeks, according to Reuters. The EU Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Chrisophe Hansen warned that food security requires more attention at all levels.” “The weaponization of food has become a reality,” he posted on X on Monday. Lescure, the French Economy Minister, allayed fears of the risk of food shortages in the country – but called on providers to bolster their cybersecurity measures. “When we discovered this cyberattack, it worried us about the ability of our distribution chains to properly deliver food to all our fellow citizens,” he said on Tuesday. “This is a wake-up call for everyone.” CNN’s Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

articles.title: Prosecutor calls Russell Brand a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator at trial
articles.summary: Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor said Wednesday as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian.
articles.body: LONDON — Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor said Wednesday as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offenses between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors at Southwark Crown Court in London that the six women, who do not know each other, were assaulted in “a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at (Brand’s) home address.” She said that at the time Brand had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and “women were simply a means to an end.” “He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said. Brand is on bail and arrived at court Wednesday to a crowd of photographers and video journalists. He said he felt “blessed.” “I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.” Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.” In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

articles.title: Guernsey States job cuts could fund diesel price drop says deputy
articles.summary: With the ongoing war in the Middle East increasing prices, one deputy is ask for duty to be frozen.
articles.body:
A Guernsey deputy has said leaders could fund a fuel price drop for drivers by cutting civil servant posts.

Deputy Neil Inder said he plans to submit two amendments around the cost of fuel in relation to the upcoming States budget amid "exceptional circumstances due to global events".

The proposed amendments are to freeze fuel duty and to also cut the cost at the pumps of white diesel - used by cars, trucks and buses - by 5p.

Asked how the States would fund this, he added: "What the States needs to start looking at properly is reducing the size of the civil service."

In the 2027 budget, fuel duty is due to increase by inflation (4.3%) from 1 January 2027, increasing duty rates to 94.4p per litre.

With the war continuing in the Middle East, fuel prices have increased across Europe, with diesel prices hitting an all-time high, according to the RAC motoring organisation.

It comes as fuel prices recently hit record highs across Guernsey, and the price of diesel hit £2.00 per litre in the UK.

White diesel, used for regular road vehicles, is subject to the standard fuel duty rate, while red diesel, used in industries including farming and fishing, is a rebated fuel that is duty-free or has a heavily reduced tax rate.

"I think we've got to realise what's happened to the world diesel prices," said Inder.

"There's been an unreasonable spike in diesel prices over the last three or four months and it really is set to get worse."

He said this would inevitably impact the cost of living and added: "Whether we like it or not diesel really does make the world go round and the wheels turn in Guernsey."

Inder said under "normal circumstances" he would probably go along with the P&R proposal to "up duty on the diesel", but said the global climate called for greater consideration.

"In reality the biggest cost to the States is the amount of people we employ," he said.

"Given the cost of the revenue they would gain, all that really is, is four or five civil servants - stop employing them, those that retire, don't replace them."

"There's only one budget a year and this is the time to address it," added Inder.

The BBC has asked the States for comment.
