articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee has rallied behind the arrested Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders, accusing the BJP-led Centre of trying to suppress democratic rights and silence young people.In a message posted on X on Wednesday, Banerjee condemned the arrests of Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were sent to judicial custody, and assured young people of her support. “Your Didi is with you - today and forever!” she wrote.The arrests came amid opposition protests in Delhi over alleged electoral irregularities and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Why the CJP leaders were arrestedDelhi Police detained CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ajinkya Shinde on Tuesday. They were accused of allegedly entering the Jantar Mantar area without authorisation and violating peace bonds signed earlier by Ranka and Das.The area was recently denotified as a designated venue for demonstrations. Police alleged that the three leaders breached barricades, entered the restricted area, raised slogans demanding Kumar's resignation and displayed the National Flag.Shinde was granted bail, while Das and Ranka were sent to five days of judicial custody after being produced before an executive magistrate on Wednesday morning. They were subsequently lodged in Tihar Jail.Mamata calls arrests an attempt to silence youthCondemning the police action, Banerjee said the fight for democratic rights had continued across generations and called on people to stand together to protect them.“We, and many generations before us, have fought strongly for our democratic rights. We must continue to do so. I strongly condemn the arrest of Ashutosh and Saurav of the CJP. These moments are about us all, pledging and standing up to fight unitedly to protect our great democracy,” she wrote on X.Banerjee described the arrests as an “attempt to intimidate and silence an entire generation” and said people must not give up their constitutional rights.“This is unacceptable. We must never surrender our constitutional rights. This murdering of democracy is happening in many parts of the country. At this moment, 14,000 of our people in Bengal are facing the brunt of police and political atrocities,” she claimed.The Trinamool Congress leader had also joined opposition protests in Delhi demanding Kumar's resignation. She backed the agitation initiated by the CJP and supported by the INDIA bloc, which has raised allegations of “vote chori” (vote theft) and electoral roll manipulation linked to the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.“A government that has forgotten that 'it is of the people, by the people, for the people' is nearing its end. To the millions of young people I say: Your Didi is with you - today and forever! Let us stand together and save our Mother India. Jai Hind! Vande Mataram! Joy Bangla!” Banerjee wrote.Opposition leaders join criticism of Delhi PoliceAbhishek Banerjee, the Diamond Harbour MP from the Mamata-led TMC faction, also criticised the arrests, accusing the BJP of targeting people for displaying the national flag.“The so-called biggest nationalists are now arresting Indians for unfurling and waving the Tricolour in their own country, an act which, according to the Union Government, constitutes a breach of peace. Welcome to the @ BJP4India's new Pakistanified Bharat,” he wrote on X.Other leaders from the faction, including Derek O'Brien and Mahua Moitra, also criticised the police action.Several opposition figures have voiced concern over the arrests, including Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, former Tamil Nadu chief minister and DMK leader MK Stalin, AAP leader and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal, CPI general secretary D Raja, NCP MP Supriya Sule and Shiv Sena (UBT) MLA Aditya Thackeray.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Big Bang Theory' producer says societies who abandon God drift toward tyranny
articles.summary: Famous producer Chuck Lorre told Joe Rogan that societies replacing God with extreme ideologies like communism or fascism becoming tyrannical and dystopian
articles.body: Hollywood producer Chuck Lorre, the creative force behind hit sitcoms such as "Two and a Half Men" and "The Big Bang Theory," discussed the importance of spirituality on Joe Rogan's podcast Tuesday. Lorre released his memoir, "Sitcom: A Memoir," on Tuesday, reflecting on his life and career. Lorre has previously discussed his religious background, having been raised Jewish before joining the Church of Scientology in his youth and later embracing Buddhism. In the most recent episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience," Lorre warned that worldly wealth and fame ultimately are not fulfilling and that "it's not the real solution. The real solution, you know, I'm going to say it and then regret it, but the real solution is a spiritual solution. You have to find something beyond this world." After Rogan asked why he might regret making the remark, including whether it had to do with working in Hollywood, Lorre replied that he didn't wish to be associated with "new age bulls---." RICHARD GERE CONFRONTS HOLLYWOOD FAME, EGO AND GREED AS 'DARK CLOUDS' THAT THREATEN INNER PEACE Rogan agreed, saying he believes the term "spirituality" has been co-opted by insincere people who have given it a "bad name." "I know some people that are like legitimately spiritual. Some of the nicest people that I know," Rogan said, describing a Christian acquaintance who built homes for homeless people and helped them overcome addiction. "It's like I know people like that too," Lorre agreed. "They're real, and they’re role models." Later on in the episode, Lorre marveled at how humans are unlike animals in that they create religions as a means of understanding and valuing the world around them, saying, "You wanna call it true or not, it's an organizing element that no other animal does." 'WIZARDS OF WAVERLY PLACE' STAR DAVID HENRIE SAYS HIS FAITH COST HIM AGENTS, MONEY AND FRIENDS IN HOLLYWOOD Lorre argued that it didn't matter if a particular religion was "true" but said that when a society abandons a belief in a supernatural god, it begins to worship extreme ideologies. "When civilizations or cultures that took God out of the picture, they replaced it, with the Communist Party, with a fascist dictator. You know, it's the same idea: ‘Organize around me. Doesn’t matter if I’m right or not, organize around me.’ And people will," he warned. Lorre compared shared religious beliefs to a tent pole holding society's understanding of reality together, suggesting that challenging those beliefs can provoke anger and uncertainty. "And if you take that away from them, they get angry. It freaks them out because it's like the tent pole. That tent pole moves, the tent comes down and everything, you know, if you believe that this is the truth and someone says, ‘No, it's not. It's bulls---.’ Everything else you believe is in fair play. Everything," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lorre himself is no stranger to political commentary. Last month at the Project Angel Food Angel Awards in Los Angeles, Lorre used his acceptance speech to insult the first family, call the president a "Russian asset" and joke about checking whether Trump had suffered a fatal heart attack. He also called the first lady "a surgically enhanced, cold-hearted Yugoslavian escort who clearly hates her husband."

articles.title: New Tata Curvv EV had a faulty charging port at delivery; buyer to get Rs 1.1 lakh and free repairs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Hyderabad consumer commission has directed Tata Motors and its dealer to replace faulty parts of a Curvv electric car free of cost and pay Rs
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Hyderabad consumer commission has directed Tata Motors and its dealer to replace faulty parts of a Curvv electric car free of cost and pay Rs 1.1 lakh to a buyer after finding that the new vehicle had a defective charging port at the time of delivery. The commission also held both companies jointly and severally liable for the compensation and litigation costs.The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-III, Hyderabad, passed the order on September 29, 2026, after finding that the electric vehicle had developed problems immediately after purchase and was repeatedly taken to service centres for repairs.BackgroundAccording to the commission order, M R Laboratories Pvt Ltd, represented by its authorised signatory Mallikharjuna Rao Mathi, booked a new Tata Curvv EV from Orange Auto on December 28, 2024, by paying Rs 21,000.The company arranged the remaining vehicle cost through a Bank of Baroda car loan dated January 6, 2025. It also paid Rs 2,92,025 towards accessories and other charges on January 8, 2025, as instructed by the dealer. The vehicle was insured on January 10, 2025.The buyer requested delivery on January 24, 2025. According to the complaint, the dealer did not deliver the vehicle as promised and cited a ritual following a death at the car showroom. The buyer was instead made to accept a hurried demonstration.During the demonstration, the vehicle’s charging port was found to be defective. The dealer assured the buyer that the problem would be fixed the next day, but no repair was carried out on January 25, 2025.The buyer alleged that the vehicle was shifted between service centres that lacked trained staff and proper equipment. The car remained at workshops from February 4 to February 15, 2025. The complaint referred to different explanations given for the problem, including a broken latch, a stuck wire, an electrical malfunction and a burnt-out motor.The buyer sent a written complaint to the dealer on February 16, 2025. It was delivered on February 19, but the buyer received no response.He then approached the consumer commission seeking replacement of the vehicle or a refund of Rs 23,13,025, along with Rs 5 lakh as compensation and Rs 50,000 towards litigation costs.What did the dealer and Tata Motors say?Orange Auto appeared through its law firm but did not file its written version within the prescribed period. The commission recorded that its right to file the response had therefore been forfeited.Tata Motors, however, opposed the complaint, arguing that M R Laboratories was not a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, because it had purchased the vehicle for business purposes.The manufacturer also argued that the dealer handled the sale, delivery, servicing and repairs, and that no manufacturing defect had been established through expert evidence. It said it had no direct role in the alleged problems with the vehicle’s delivery and repairs and should not have been made a party to the complaint.What did the commission find?The bench comprising President M Ramgopal Reddy and members J Shyamala and D Sreedevi found that the buyer qualified as a consumer because Tata Motors had not produced documentary evidence showing that the vehicle was being used for commercial transport or a profit-generating fleet.The commission noted that the charging port, an essential part of an electric vehicle, was found to be defective at the time of delivery. It also took into account the repeated repair attempts and the dealer’s failure to file its written response.“The uncontroverted facts reveal that the vehicle's charging port-the absolute lifeline of an Electric Vehicle was dysfunctional at the exact time of delivery (24.01.2025),” the commission said.It further observed that the dealer had failed to address the allegations through a written response. The commission treated this, along with the evidence on record, as supporting the buyer’s complaint about the defective vehicle and the dealer’s service.The commission also considered Tata Motors’ argument that the buyer had not established a manufacturing defect through expert evidence. It noted that no expert opinion from an authorised laboratory or authority had been produced to establish a manufacturing defect that would justify replacement of the entire vehicle or a refund of its price.“Since the vehicle has spent an extensive period under experimental repairs immediately post-delivery, both Opp.parties are jointly and severally liable as the manufacturer produces the goods, and the dealer serves as its market conduit,” the bench said.The commission concluded that the buyer was entitled to relief for the inconvenience and mental agony caused by the supply of a vehicle with defects. It directed the companies to replace the faulty parts at no cost rather than order replacement of the entire vehicle or a refund of its price.Final orderThe consumer commission partly allowed the complaint in its September 29, 2026 order and directed Tata Motors and Orange Auto, jointly and severally, to:Replace the faulty parts of the Tata Curvv EV at zero cost.Pay Rs 1 lakh as compensation for mental agony.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The commission dismissed the remaining claims, including the request for replacement of the entire vehicle or a refund of its full price.The companies were directed to comply within 45 days of receiving a copy of the order.

articles.title: State Department issues travel advisory as arrests and exit bans hit popular destination
articles.summary: The U.S. State Department's Level 3 Saudi Arabia travel advisory cites terrorism, missile attacks and strict social media laws as key concerns for those considering trips there.
articles.body: Americans who may be planning an overseas trip are facing an updated warning from the U.S. State Department amid heightened safety and security concerns. The department issued a Level 3 "Reconsider Travel" advisory for Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12 — with certain parts of the country carrying the more severe Level 4 "Do Not Travel" designation. U.S. officials cited several concerns behind the warning — including regional conflict, terrorism, missile and drone attacks, exit bans and strict laws surrounding social media activity. AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION The updated advisory comes after a series of attacks on Saudi airports by Iran-backed Houthi rebels reportedly killed at least 14 people, including an American, and injured more than 300 others, as Fox News Digital recently reported. "I would probably sit it out." Travel expert Lee Abbamonte told Fox News Digital, "Americans considering travel to Saudi Arabia should be aware of fresh attacks on Riyadh airport and threats of further action due to conflict with the Houthis and the ongoing Iran war." He added, "This is a very confusing time for Saudi travel, as we don’t currently know where this conflict will go. I would probably sit it out if I were thinking of traveling to the region" right now. The security concerns have also affected commercial air travel, according to the department. The threat of Iranian missile and drone attacks has continued since hostilities between the U.S. and Iran began in February, the State Department said. Commercial flights are still operating in Saudi Arabia, though service has faced major disruptions at times. Cities, airports, military bases, energy facilities and other infrastructure have been targeted, while debris from intercepted weapons can also pose a danger to people on the ground. Travelers are also being cautioned about what they capture on their phones during such incidents. "Do not photograph, film or share information about missile or drone interceptions or impact sites," the State Department warned — noting that Americans have been detained for taking photos of recent events. Terrorism remains another concern. Officials are warning that attacks could happen with little or no warning at tourist attractions, hotels, transportation hubs, shopping malls and other places visited by foreigners. The advisory also cautions Americans about what they post or interact with on social media. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "Some U.S. citizens have been arrested for past social media activity," the advisory states. That can include posts, reposts or likes viewed as critical of the Saudi government or its leaders, even if they were shared while outside the country, according to the department. The advisory warns that violating Saudi laws, even unintentionally, can carry serious consequences. "If you break laws in Saudi Arabia — even by mistake — you could be deported, fined, imprisoned or subject to an exit ban," the advisory states. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The strongest warning applies near the Yemen border, where Americans are advised not to travel due to terrorism. For those who do travel to Saudi Arabia, officials recommend staying alert, following local news and having a plan to leave in an emergency without depending on U.S. government assistance. Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional comment and details. A State Department spokesperson confirmed to The Travel that the U.S. Mission in Saudi Arabia issued a separate security alert on October 10, strongly urging all Americans to avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the surrounding areas, the outlet reported. articles.title: Trump: ‘Massive’ oil, gas, mineral exploration set to begin in Greenland
articles.summary: President Trump announced early Wednesday that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is “getting ready to begin” in Greenland. The president’s brief post on Truth Social pointed to the Danish territory’s plentiful oil supplies and natural resources but offered few details about the new initiative. “There are Experts that are saying that the amount of…
articles.body:
President Trump announced early Wednesday that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is “getting ready to begin” in Greenland .

The president’s brief post on Truth Social pointed to the Danish territory’s plentiful oil supplies and natural resources but offered few details about the new initiative.

“There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World and, even more importantly, from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe, is second to none,” Trump wrote overnight.

“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he continued. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!”

The announcement follows his administration’s decision to enter into a security agreement last month with Denmark and Greenland, which sought to calm tensions between the two sides after Trump repeatedly threatened to seize the Arctic island.

The deal was largely aimed toward strengthening military readiness in the region, allowing the U.S. to expand military bases in the territory. It also includes provisions on resource extraction and “minerals cooperation” for the involved parties.

However, Greenland’s deputy mining minister Jørgen Hammeken-Holm rejected the immediacy of the president’s announcement, telling CNN in an interview that the island was “very far away from ‘massive’ exploration.”

“There are many smaller explorations underway, but these could take years to become operational,” he added, referencing the issues researchers have encountered in attempting to obtain Greenland’s natural resources.

Rare earth minerals in the region are often encased in rock, and the offshore oil and gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice, making extraction expensive and labor-intensive.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
articles.summary: With few details so far, it is unclear what might need to change for a Pope who has been focused on stability.
articles.body:
Vatican transparency about papal health has come a long way from the secrecy of the past.

But that does not mean Catholics were prepared for such seismic news about cancer and removal of a large section of Pope Leo XIV's lung - even after he announced on Sunday that doctors had discovered a nodule.

On Tuesday, the 71-year-old was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following 90-minute surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.

Part of the shock has, of course, been because there had been few signs until now that concern was needed about any imminent risks to the Pope's health.

A member of the Order of St Augustine, a saint who placed great importance on developing good habits, the Pope is known to place great importance in good habits, including when it comes to health and fitness, such as weekly games of tennis.

Now, with so many unknowns about the pontiff's prognosis and what treatment he might need, questions swirl around what may have to change in his routine, and for how long.

Certainly, given the dangers surrounding air travel soon after lung surgery, and the high altitude of some of the stops involved, a November trip to South America – including to Peru, the country Pope Leo called home for more than 20 years – may be in doubt.

His predecessor, Francis, once wrote that he had started his papacy thinking he might only have a few years in the role, having already suffered health complications throughout his life.

As such, it was clear that he was intent on making waves quickly and implementing what some saw as fairly radical change in the Church at a swift pace.

While Pope Leo's papacy has undoubtedly started in what appears to be a comparatively measured way, he has still grown quickly into being a powerful, uncompromising and compassionate moral voice on the world stage.

His messaging in opposition to war , in support of the dignity of migrants and on the dangers of AI in particular has stood out in its clarity.

To some extent, he has already done what many Catholics had feared was barely possible, in starting to bring closer together different factions of a Church that had seemed somewhat divided.

Noticeably, both progressive and traditionalist followers often talking of him as a voice that reflects their own.

But even after successful surgery, and with no details yet about what happens now, speculation has already begun as to whether a cancer diagnosis will mean an evident shift in Pope Leo's pace in implementing changes he sees as necessary.

On the other hand any dramatic moves, such as on doctrine, would certainly feel out of character for a Pope who for nearly a year and a half has shown himself to be measured, thoughtful and discerning, as well as having a focus on stability.

articles.title: Mexico should rethink its dangerous partnerships with Chinese telecoms
articles.summary: The proximity of these companies to the U.S.-Mexico border represents an imminent danger to the security of both nations.
articles.body:
Huawei , the Chinese telecom giant banned in the U.S. and Europe , seeks to strengthen ties with Mexico. In recent months, Mexico’s secretary of Science and Technology , secretary of Energy , Anti-Corruption secretary and members of the Mexican Senate have held key meetings with senior executives from the Chinese firm.

The new head of Huawei Mexico, David Tao, has made it clear that the company wants to deepen and expand their operations in telecommunications, power grids and artificial intelligence.

During the last two decades , Huawei has generated bipartisan concern in America. The company has been charged with allegations including espionage , racketeering and conspiracy to steal American trade secrets. Huawei has denied this and other allegations against it.

Despite this background, Huawei has increased its growth fivefold in Mexico since 2022, has invested $64 million in the country and has installed a technical support center that covers Mexico and Latin America.

Mexico — America’s neighbor and largest trading partner — has also welcomed a Chinese state-owned telecommunications company, Unicom, offering it a broad license to operate freely for 30 years. Huawei and Unicom maintain close cooperation in promoting AI in sectors such as government and manufacturing in different countries.

Huawei has been charged with violating U.S. sanctions by working with North Korea and Iran . Last year, the European Parliament shut down a major infiltration of Huawei’s lobbyists into one of the most important centers of political power in the region. Authorities reported cases of bribery and corruption involving the communist technological giant.

Huawei has managed to position itself as a leader in 5G technology. However, it remains under the shadow of distrust due to allegations of control and collection of private and highly sensitive information. In 2019, the Trump administration instructed all government agencies to eradicate the use of telecommunication equipment made by Huawei because this technology presented a serious threat to national security.

The Chinese company grew under the approval of the Communist Party. It was officially launched in 1987 and during the years has grown from a telephone importer to a global conglomerate valued at $178 billion with a presence in 170 countries.

China and its spy bases in Cuba also ratified the strategy against the U.S. In recent years, there have been reports of activities by Huawei and Chinese telecommunications company ZTE in Cuba, including in areas near the location of spy bases.

Let’s be clear: Huawei is not only a threat to national security but also to commercial activity. Economic integrity and supply chain security are often casualties of China’s commercial ambition. All the so-called private companies in China have to submit to the unquestionable powers of the Chinese Communist Party.

This is not just trade. The proximity of these companies to the U.S.-Mexico border represents an imminent danger to the security of both nations.

Last week, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced that it will vote to bolster telecom border security with Mexico and Canada. The rules would also enhance foreign ownership reporting, mandate disclosures on the use of untrusted equipment or service providers and require carriers to adhere to cybersecurity standards, among other measures.

While the U.S. seeks to improve its telecom security, Mexico must reverse and review its relationship with the Chinese company that wants to expand its technological eyes and ears at the border. This is the right time to make the right decisions.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.title: Ukraine says new Starlink restrictions disrupt military as it reels from intel gaps and Trump clash
articles.summary: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.
articles.body: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies. Facing pressure from President Donald Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried Washington could cut off battlefield support to try and force it into concessions at the negotiating table. Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week caused confusion, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News. Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intel, but with relations spiraling Ukrainian officials and military units were on Wednesday accusing SpaceX of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations. It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally. Drone disruptions SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov. “Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added. An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations. The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control. “The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement. Beskrestnov said that restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph. Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he added. Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s Charge d’Affaires to the U.S. Denys Sienik said “the technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.” Ukraine has reached out to the U.S. government and SpaceX for clarification on the rationale for the new restrictions but has yet to receive a response, according to a Ukrainian official. Ukraine’s armed forces learned about the limitations from customer support after filing a complaint regarding operational issues, the official said, adding that SpaceX had not warned of the move. Ukrainian military units were already reporting issues with drone performance at even lower speeds, the official added. The White House and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News. The disruption follows days of mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington, as Trump pushes to lower gas prices ahead of the midterm elections. Trump’s latest reversal in his bid to settle the war saw him stun Kyiv by striking a diesel deal with Russia that upended years of U.S. sanctions. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. Trump also announced an “energy ceasefire” that neither warring side appears to have agreed to. Kyiv said it had refrained from striking Russian energy targets to respect Trump’s wishes, but the Kremlin has continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in its annual effort to leave its neighbor in the freezing dark as winter sets in. Intel uncertainty Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had not received any early warning from its partners about “a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv” a day earlier. Explosions rang out before an alert was issued, according to an NBC News producer in the capital. “Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues,” Zelenskyy said, without singling out the U.S. Later Tuesday, he reported another strike on Kyiv was “the second time Ukraine was not warned.” Since Russia invaded Ukraine more than four years ago, the U.S. has provided significant satellite and eavesdropping intelligence to Kyiv. European partners also share intelligence with Kyiv, but Ukrainian officials see the U.S. intelligence assistance as crucial to their fight against Russia. Trump denied withholding information critical to Ukraine’s defense, despite reported threats to cut off U.S. intelligence if Kyiv failed to stop its attacks on Russian refineries. “We are helping them and we are sharing intel,” the president told reporters Tuesday. After the first Russian attack Monday, when five ballistic missiles were able to strike civilian infrastructure without advance notice from the U.S., two Ukrainian officials told NBC News it was the result of a technical issue, or glitch, in U.S. intelligence sharing. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also reassured the audience that U.S. intelligence sharing continued, blaming the delayed alert on a “special type of the weaponry” used by Russia. But after the second attack Tuesday, Ukrainian and European officials said the reason was less clear. “We didn’t receive warning for a second time, and this doesn’t look like a coincidence,” one of the Ukrainian officials said. The second Ukrainian official attributed the issue to bad weather. Two European officials told NBC News they were still trying to understand why there was no advance notice. Ukrainian air force spokesman Col. Yurii Ihnat said Wednesday that after the second ballistic strike on Kyiv without a warning, “in the next three waves of attacks, notifications from partners about the use of ballistic weapons did come through.” The Kremlin noted the confusion Wednesday, but said it was “too early to draw any systemic conclusions.” Zelenskyy said that at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were without power Wednesday after the latest wave of Russian attacks, adding that President Vladimir Putin was in clear violation of the energy truce announced by Trump. “Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he added. Like Trump, Musk has repeatedly oscillated in his stance on the war. The billionaire turned on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become a lifeline for war-torn parts of the country, but has also facilitated battlefield communications ​and enabled the use of longer-range drones, given its resistance to signal jamming. Musk agreed to ​turn off thousands of Russian-used Starlinks in Ukraine this year, causing problems ‌for ⁠the Kremlin’s forces. But in recent days, Musk has echoed Trump’s criticism. The suggestion that his company might have deliberately limited Ukraine’s battlefield operations drew criticism in Europe. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote in a post on X, referencing a past clash over Starlink in which Musk called him a “small man.” Sikorski continued; “As your European customers, we are watching you.”

articles.title: Waterford: Vehicles and devices seized after four murders
articles.summary: Searches take place at several premises in Waterford after four family members die in a arson attack.
articles.body:
Searches have been carried out at a number of premises in Waterford after four members of the same family were killed an arson attack in the city.

Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue was set on fire on Tuesday.

Gardaí (Irish police) have described the investigation into their murders as "intense in nature and very active".

They said "multiple searches" were conducted on Tuesday evening and a number of vehicles and electronic devices have been seized for technical examination.

Six members of the English family were sleeping when their home was attacked in the early hours of Tuesday.

It is believed that an incendiary device, likely a petrol bomb, set the house on fire.

Two children were severely injured in the blaze and were taken to a Dublin hospital where they both remain in a critical condition.

Members of the local community have been supporting their relatives and some have been sharing poignant memories of those who did not survive the fire.

For the past five years, Callum played football for Johnville FC, a schoolboy and junior football club in Waterford.

His coach Alex O'Sullivan told BBC News NI that he was a "fantastic player" and a "lovely kid" both on and off the pitch.

"Great sense of humour... always happy. Helpful to his teammates and coaches. There was never any cheek coming from Callum.

"You'd often see him on the street and he'd be waving, 'Hello coach', and you'd get a little chat out of him, and he always had a great smile on his face."

O'Sullivan said he first met Callum when he was playing under-11s football.

"Callum was always there. Same with matches, he loved coming to the matches."

O'Sullivan said he also got to know the boy's parents Phillip and Kim, from dropping Callum off to training and supporting him when he was playing.

O'Sullivan said the community and club were "devastated".

"There has been a dark cloud over St John's Park.

"Usually there's always people with a smile on their face around St John's Park. Everyone is sad today."

In a statement on social media, Johnville FC said all its members were "absolutely heartbroken"

"It is incredibly difficult to comprehend that a family we knew so well has been taken from us in such tragic circumstances."

The Catholic Diocese of Waterford and Lismore has confirmed that a vigil will be held at Sacred Heart Church on Wednesday evening.

In a post on social media, the diocese said the vigil will provide an opportunity for people to "come together in prayer for those who have lost their lives, their grieving families and loved ones, and all those affected by this terrible tragedy".

Gardaí launched an investigation into the four killings on Tuesday, describing it as a "multiple murder and arson attack".

Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting that detectives believe the attack is linked to organised crime and drugs-related intimidation.

It said the searches carried out in the city on Tuesday night included raids on properties of two significant criminal figures in the city.

On Wednesday, Ch Supt Anthony Pettit said: "There are people in the community who know the person or persons who carried out this arson attack in which four people have been murdered."

He appealed for them to contact the investigation team, which is based at Waterford Garda Station.

On Tuesday morning, firefighters, ambulance staff and gardaí all responded to the emergency at the family home in the Birchwood housing estate, about 3km (1.8 miles) outside Waterford city centre.

Waterford Fire Service said it was alerted to the fire at 05:13 local time and its crews arrived to a well-developed fire at a two-storey house.

It said a number of casualties were removed from the house before the blaze was extinguished and the scene was handed over to gardaí.

On Tuesday afternoon, Ch Supt Pettit said officers believe the house "was attacked by a person or persons unknown and that the fire was started deliberately".

He appealed to anyone who was in the vicinity of the Birchwood housing estate between 04.30 and 05.30 local time on Tuesday morning to contact gardaí.

articles.title: Look of the Week: Ayo Edebiri’s swan silhouette reimagines the bustle
articles.summary: The “Clarissa” star appeared at the London Film Festival in a Chanel skirt set that looked radically different, depending on your angle.
articles.body: I often base my impression of a celebrity on one of two major variables: how much I would want to actually be their friend and yap over martinis and French fries or how much I would want to raid their closet. The Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning actor Ayo Edebiri passes both tests. For her latest public outing, a screening of her upcoming film “Clarissa” at the London Film Festival, the actor wore a sophisticated number from Chanel, courtesy of the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy. Featuring a sleek black column skirt and minimalist stilettos, the look, while pared- back, was far from boring thanks to a creamy sleeveless top with a voluminous feather-like hem. Edebiri’s dangling earrings also provided a welcome pop of color, with their wine-hue complementing her berry lipstick. Her flowing braids were twisted into an elegant cascading updo with two skinny strands framing her face. Even while dripping in haute couture, Edebiri somehow never appears stuffy or unapproachable — quite the opposite. While yes, she’s a newly appointed brand ambassador for Chanel, so it is quite literally her job to look good in whatever she’s given to wear, she, along with her longtime stylist Danielle Goldberg, always manage to make the label’s creations appear breezy, youthful and relaxed. The look was originally part of Chanel’s Haute Couture Spring-Summer 2026 collection, which leaned heavily into fairytales and woodland magic. (The avian motifs appeared again at Blazy’s show earlier this month at Paris Fashion Week, where gargantuan bird sculptures floated over showgoers heads.) It’s only when looking at Edebiri’s outfit from the side however, that the swan-esque silhouette reveals itself, almost presenting as a modern-day bustle. Edebiri’s look brings to mind musician Bjork’s quite literal interpretation of a swan dress at the 2001 Academy Awards; an outfit cemented in pop culture history as one of the red carpet’s most referenced, albeit campy, moments. Twenty-five years on, Edebiri’s own swan style is sleek and elegant, but still playful. (And we know Edebiri is a Bjork fan!) Fittingly, birds are also a recurring motif in Virginia’s Woolf’s “Mrs. Dalloway,” which serves as the source material for Edebiri’s new movie, “Clarissa.” In the 1925 novel, the appearance of fledglings symbolizes freedom, confinement and even spiritual rebirth, themes that follow lead characters Clarissa and Sally (whom Edebiri portrays) as the story unfolds. “Clarissa” is one of the year’s most stylish cinematic offerings thanks to the lush landscape of its reimagined setting in Nigeria, as well as the thoughtful costuming curated by Eniola Dawodu. (The rest of the film’s cast deserve their fashion flowers as well, with India Amarteifio and Sophie Okonedo wearing the likes of Prada, Luar, and Georges Hobeika during the movie’s festival appearances.) It’s safe to assume that Edebiri and her co-stars will sartorially honor the film’s artistry on many red carpets to come.

articles.title: Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
articles.summary: One official claims satellite internet could erode online governance in Iran amid war with the US and Israel.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have pledged to continue a crackdown against satellite internet service Starlink, along with further restrictions on the global internet as the US-Israel war on Iran continues.

Elon Musk’s Starlink, which is free of the heavy filtering and restrictions imposed by Tehran, is outlawed in Iran on national security grounds. The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment.

It is one of the many measures imposed by Iranian authorities since the United States and Israel launched strikes on the country on February 28, leading to a prolonged and economically punishing war between the countries.

Iran’s 90 million people have undergone two lengthy state-imposed global internet shutdowns in 2026 – for three weeks during nationwide protests in January and for 88 days at the start of the ongoing war .

Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council, described Starlink as a “tool of war” for enemies.

“It is a tool used for command and control by the enemy, for espionage and information gathering,” he said. “We have several systems for cutting off Starlink satellite terminals.”

He did not elaborate on what measures or devices were being used to block Starlink, but one was deployed during the January protests and authorities were prepared to share the technology with aligned countries.

Iran is among several countries that have banned or restricted Starlink due to national security concerns.

It has set baseline sentences of between six months and two years for using or possessing Starlink. Importing and distributing the devices carry jail terms of up to five years. If paired with national security or espionage charges, individuals can even face the death penalty.

Aghamiri has called on Iranians to use domestic platforms, supported by what the authorities call the National Information Network. He also backed a tiered-access model, which envisages protected international access for selected groups – such as traders, researchers and journalists – during periods of internet restrictions.

A Tehran-based internet and telecommunications expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Al Jazeera that Iranian authorities use a combination of measures to block Starlink connections.

This includes the use of multiple jammers with different configurations to disrupt services, along with spoofed GPS locations to slow new devices being set up. They can also identify Starlink-associated internet protocols if they connect to local applications and services.

Authorities also try to physically intercept terminals using patrols and drone searches, or raid locations selling the terminals.

In June, Israeli politician Naftali Bennett claimed that Israel had smuggled tens of thousands of Starlink devices into Iran when he was prime minister, between 2021 and 2022, to aid antigovernment protesters.

Since 2023, Iran has also pursued the matter at the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, trying to pressure the US and Norway, which plays a role in the satellite network’s regulatory filings, to halt transmissions.

On October 4, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Norwegian ambassador in Tehran to protest against what it described as a failure to act over unauthorised Starlink operations.

During a governance meeting at the end of September, Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami had warned authorities that Starlink could signify “the last nail in the coffin of the [cyberspace] governance” of Iran if it becomes prevalent, due to the unfettered internet access it provides.

He pointed out that the government blocked the messaging app Telegram after the cost-of-living protests in 2017-18, but had to resort to a weeklong internet shutdown for the first time during the nationwide protests in 2019 . WhatsApp and Instagram were blocked after the 2022-23 protests, which preceded the near-total shutdown during the January 2026 protests.

“If this trend continues, in the next crisis we will have to cut electricity, because Starlink, as a new tool of evading state governance, is fundamentally not even dependent on our network,” Hakami said.

Starlink has allowed Iranians to send out videos of the protests abroad since 2022 despite state restrictions. Tens of thousands of terminals are believed to have been smuggled into the country since, but exact figures are unknown.

Due to the risk of a state crackdown, limited availability and financial costs, most people still have no access to Starlink and must rely on Iran’s domestic internet, which blocks most international services and thousands of websites. US sanctions and banking restrictions further impede Iranians’ access to global services.

To circumvent the many roadblocks, most Iranians use virtual private networks (VPNs) and other methods that grant access to the free internet. But those tools can reduce connection speeds, prove costly or provide unsafe connections that jeopardise user data, and become harder to come by during periods of state-imposed internet blackout.

According to the authorities, more restrictions were possible in the future if the war intensifies, after a relative decrease in violence since the June memorandum of understanding, which eventually lapsed without a permanent ceasefire, between the US and Iran.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told a news conference on Tuesday that state bodies were deliberately disrupting the internet ostensibly to protect people and national assets from cyberattacks.

“It is obvious that due to the importance of our databases and internet-based services, decision-making bodies are sometimes forced to bring down internet speeds,” she said. “We don’t deny this issue.”

The authorities claim that they have considered removing restrictions on some platforms, although no action has been taken yet.

State-linked media late on Tuesday released a policy and governance framework document that the cyberspace council’s Aghamiri said has been under consideration for nearly two years but remained confidential due to security concerns.

The document offered no timeline for reopening any platform, and media reports said implementation had been halted by wars and protests.

The document says Google Play and WhatsApp could potentially be unblocked, while YouTube and Telegram would have to negotiate with Iran and accept certain conditions determined by the authorities to be unblocked. Such steps by the social media giants are considered extremely unlikely.

articles.title: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants
articles.summary: All of the spots are in South Australia, spanning Adelaide and its surrounding wine regions.
articles.body:
Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction in the guide's first selection for the country.

Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.

South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.

The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.

Over the past decade, Michelin has discussed bringing the guide to the country with the national tourism board several times, but without success.

South Australia decided to go it alone and pursue its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with the broadcaster.

"It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.

The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.

Created by brothers Andre and Edouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition.

Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world.

One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey.

Among the one-star recipients is Arkhé in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list:

The wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices.
